t: Semester Two and New for the Sake of New
q: The answer, of course, is that there's not a ton of new in my book, just like there's not much new on this blog. You and I don't tend to need new — we need permission to focus, permission to jump off the hamster wheel and just think. New for the sake of new is kind of crazy — long-term flourishing is what we're after, not new.

Part of this is probably the marketing machine we're marinating in each day. There's a market incentive for creating new and improved, and so there are advertising dollars and teams of smart people aiming, every day, at getting you and me to buy the idea that what we need is something new, something that we just haven't quite bought yet.

Another reason might be that we're impatient — it's easier to move toward the Next Thing than it is to keep coming back to the same old sandbox. The trouble with our impatience, of course, is that it's so likely to lead us astray. After all, the sandboxes we've been digging in for months or years may just be the ones to camp out in for decades, getting a little bit better at them all the time.

So far, I've been amazed at how much better my students argue when I give them a chance to become knowledgeable on the topic first. I mean, I know that knowing things makes you think better, but it's still just sort of magical to see it happen.

This one's a stretch goal, but I'd love to get my general world history kids to read 50 different primary source documents in semester two. We had to be close to that in semester one, but I did a poor job keeping track of the number.

I'll be writing about these in the months to come, but my point in this post is to push you to resist the undertow toward new. New doesn't make sense unless what we're already doing really, really won't work.
They'll get stronger, and so will I. And think of all the time I'll save not seeking the next big thing to occupy my time and attention. I'll focus, and I'll get better.

Staying in the same few sandboxes for years, getting slightly better each time, beats rotating through initiatives.

q: There was a part of me during those first years — and still is a part of me, sometimes — that wanted to believe that the right thing — the right speech, the right unit, the right instructional approach, the right words — was all it would take to create an impactful classroom. If I could just find “it,” then I'd finally see my students getting the kinds of results I was hoping for.

The reality, it turns out, is a little disappointing, especially for teachers who want to be special and stand out. (In other words, teachers who aren't yet aware of the work beneath the work.) The key to being a great teacher is this: faithfully show up and do the right work.

It requires cultivating an integrated, poised life, one in which the way that we're working aligns with the priorities we profess. For me, I'm most able to show up fully to work when I'm loving my wife and children the way I want to be loving them, and I'm only able to do that when I'm thinking sharply about my work and the constraints I've placed around it.

First of all, the right work can't be many of the things we're expected to do because the sum of all the things we're expected to do is more than any one person can actually do. And so the first step to doing the right work is figuring out what the wrong work is — and that's typically the kind of thing that you learn on the job.

We should never become teachers who dismiss everything we're presented with at staff meetings or professional development — cynicism isn't part of the calling. But we should always ask about the costs of new initiatives: If I start doing X, what will happen to Y and Z?

Kids tend to grow, and their flourishing tends to be advanced. And, sure, the high-stakes tests happen to go our way more than they should, too. But the tests aren't what I'm after — I'm just after faithfully showing up and doing the right work, today and then the same thing tomorrow.
x: Silver bullet syndrome, the hope that one perfect speech or program will transform a classroom, is the mistake most new teachers make.
His mature conclusion is deliberately unglamorous: the key to great teaching is to faithfully show up and do the right work.
Showing up well depends on an integrated personal life in which how you work matches the priorities you profess.
Doing the right work requires first identifying the wrong work, meaning initiatives furthest removed from kids' long-term flourishing, without sliding into cynicism about PD.
Teachers cannot do everything they are asked, so the key skill is discerning wrong work, while still asking the cost of any new initiative to the work that matters.
Great teaching comes from the unexciting discipline of showing up and doing the right work day after day, not from standing out.

q: When you approach a problem by first stripping it down to its most elemental parts, that's a “first principles” approach to problem-solving.

The relationship between Great Britain and the thirteen colonies was fraught with debate and complexity in 1776, and to explain their solution to that knotty mess, the founders laid out their first principles:
Here's the point: First principles make it possible for us to see opportunities where others see an impasse. They let us think clearly in the face of interminable complexity.
Schools exist to promote the long-term flourishing of students. This is the core of our work, beneath the philosophical debates and stylistic differences and policy wars and standards and so on.
In light of the perpetual onslaught of initiatives and fads and research and “research” and tasks and minutiae we face daily, we must be clear on the first principle of education.
Long-term flourishing (or LTF, as my colleagues and I sometimes refer to it) — that's what we do. May it be emblazoned on our hearts as a charm against the overwhelm.

t: How To Drastically Improve Your Class
q: If ever your students aren’t giving you what you want . . . Stop them in their tracks. Reteach your expectations. Begin again.
Trotting it out every once in a while—or even more often than not—is not only confusing to students, but it sends the message that you don’t really mean what you say.
The strategy works because it forces you, as a natural consequence, to become extraordinarily effective with your initial instruction.
Your students may be so used to half listening, or not listening at all, that you'll have to repeat nearly everything you do.
Your students will realize that when you give an instruction, when you teach and model what you want in explicit detail, or just make a simple request, you really do mean for them to follow it.
It starts with an all-or-nothing commitment to mean what you say, to make your actions congruent with your words.
x: A simple, consistently applied secret—stop, reteach, begin again whenever expectations aren't met—can dramatically improve a class.
He explains that the strategy only works when applied consistently every single time, since inconsistent use confuses students and signals that the teacher doesn't mean what they say.
Commitment to the approach forces teachers to become more effective at initial instruction, not just more strict with consequences.

t: Why It's Okay To Be Weird
q: It doesn’t mean you must dampen your enthusiasm or become a robot when you step in front of your students.
Students are drawn to uniqueness, to teachers who are unabashedly themselves. They want to be around them, learn from them, and follow where they lead.
There is no passion in trying to be someone you’re not. You can fake it, but there will always be something missing.
Students don’t trust teachers who put on a show of perfection in their demeanor, manner, tone, and style.
It’s not uncommon for bright, funny, lovely people to change drastically the moment the morning bell rings.
Just being you, on the other hand, embracing your weird and wonderful self, unapologetically, is your greatest strength.
